samples.summary: Web (browser) OAuth callback has no CSRF `state` — login CSRF / session fixation remains fully open while the CLI half is hardened
samples.evidence:
`githubAuthCallback` only consumes a state token when the query carries one (line 119). Every browser login arrives with no `state`: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` (github.strategy.ts:59-62) sets `opts.state` *only* when `req.__cliStateToken` is present, and `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` only mints that token for `mode === 'cli'` (github-auth.guard.ts:33). So the web branch at auth.controller.ts:146-150 mints tokens and calls `setAuthCookies` for any `code` presented, with nothing binding the code to the browser that started the flow.

Attack: attacker starts a GitHub OAuth flow for their own account, stops at the redirect and captures `code=X`, then gets the victim to load `https://<backend>/auth/github/callback?code=X` (image, iframe, link). The victim's browser receives `Set-Cookie: wafflebase_session=<attacker's JWT>` (httpOnly, SameSite=Lax — a top-level navigation carries it fine) and is redirected to FRONTEND_URL. The victim now works inside the attacker's account: everything they create, upload or paste lands in a workspace the attacker owns.

This is pre-existing and the diff itself adds a risk-table row (`docs/design/rest-api.md`) marking it **Open**. I am reporting it because the change hardens exactly this class of attack on the CLI leg while leaving the higher-traffic browser leg unbound, and an acknowledged-in-docs vulnerability is still a vulnerability.
searchedFor: grep createState( across packages to find every state-minting site
checked GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate for a non-CLI state path

samples.summary: CSV formula neutralization is explicitly disabled on `sheets export`, the one path that writes a file a user opens in Excel — CSV injection survives there
samples.evidence:
`formatCsv(res.data, { neutralizeFormulas: false })` opts the file-writing path out of the defense added in this diff. The exported rows are `{ ref, value, formula }` (see the new test at packages/cli/test/sheets-export.test.ts:57-63), and the `value` column is attacker-settable independently of `formula`: a workspace collaborator can call `sheets cells set <doc> A1 '=cmd|\'/c calc\'!A0'` *without* `--formula`, storing that string as a literal value. `sheets export doc out.csv` then writes it unquoted and unprefixed; opening out.csv in Excel/LibreOffice evaluates it (DDE / HYPERLINK data exfiltration or command execution on the exporting user's machine).

The stated reason — round-tripping through `sheets import` — only requires the `formula` column to stay verbatim; neutralizing the `value` column (or neutralizing on export and teaching `sheets import` to strip a leading `'`) would preserve the pipeline. As written, the render path that prints to a terminal is protected while the path that produces an .csv file on disk is not, which is the inverse of the risk ordering.

Note this is not a regression — `formatCsv` never neutralized before — but the change consciously routes this call site around the new defense, so the mitigation reads as complete when it is not.
searchedFor: grep formatCsv across packages to enumerate all callers
read packages/cli/test/sheets-export.test.ts for the exported column shape

samples.summary: `FORMULA_TRIGGER` omits leading space/NUL/LF, a documented neutralization bypass in importers that trim leading whitespace
samples.evidence: `const FORMULA_TRIGGER = /^[=+\-@\t\r]/;` covers the OWASP core set but not a leading ASCII space. LibreOffice's Text Import has a "Trim spaces" option and several importers (and Google Sheets paste) strip leading whitespace before evaluating, so a server-supplied value of `" =HYPERLINK(\"http://evil\",\"click\")"` passes `neutralizeFormula` untouched (position 0 is a space) and can still be evaluated after the importer trims. `\n` and `\0` are likewise absent, though those are less likely to be trimmed into a formula. Suggest trimming leading whitespace before applying the trigger test, or adding `\s\0` to the character class.
searchedFor: read packages/cli/test/output.test.ts formula-neutralization cases (no leading-space case present)

samples.summary: A malformed CLI nonce is silently dropped instead of rejected, producing an unbound login and a misleading "your server is too old" diagnostic
samples.evidence: `parseCliNonce(req.query?.nonce)` returns `undefined` for any value outside `[0-9a-f]{32,128}` and the guard proceeds to `createState(mode, portNum, undefined)`. The callback then omits `state` entirely (auth.controller.ts:131-133), and the CLI refuses with `REFUSAL.noState` — "the server is likely older than this CLI — update the server" (login.ts:190-194). So a client that sends a nonce the backend dislikes (different alphabet, wrong length, or a value mangled by a proxy) is told to downgrade/upgrade the *server*, when the real cause is a rejected nonce. The flow still fails closed on a current CLI, so impact is limited to misdiagnosis, but the security-relevant part is that the server accepts an unbound CLI login rather than answering 400 — an operator watching for "is the nonce binding actually in effect?" gets no signal at all.

samples.summary: The `Origin`-header check is documented as a CSRF defense but blocks nothing an attacker would actually send
samples.evidence: `if (req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined)` refuses cross-origin requests. Browsers do not attach `Origin` to the request shapes an attacker would use against a loopback callback: a top-level navigation, an ``/`
searchedFor: read docs/design/cli.md login-flow prose in the diff

samples.summary: Loopback callback server does not validate the `Host` header — reachable via DNS rebinding
samples.evidence: The request handler builds `new URL(req.url ?? '/', 'http://127.0.0.1')`, discarding whatever `Host` the client sent, and never checks it. A remote page on `evil.test` whose DNS rebinds to 127.0.0.1 becomes same-origin with the callback server for the 30-second window and can read responses. I could not complete an exploit chain: the 200 body is a static success page and the 403 bodies are the fixed `REFUSAL` strings, so nothing secret is readable, and the nonce still gates acceptance of a `code`. Reporting as hardening — rejecting requests whose `Host` is not `127.0.0.1:<port>`/`localhost:<port>` costs one line and removes the rebinding surface entirely.
searchedFor: grep for headers.host / Host validation in packages/cli/src
checked response bodies served on both the accept and refuse paths for secret content

samples.summary: Any web page can flood the user's terminal with refusal lines and overwrite the real timeout diagnostic
samples.evidence: `refuse()` does `console.error(...)` and sets `lastRefusal` on every rejected hit, with no rate limit and no cap. During the 30-second window a page the victim visits can issue unlimited `GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=x` requests: each prints a line to stderr (scrolling away the OAuth URL the user may need to copy in a headless environment) and overwrites `lastRefusal`, so the timeout error at line 338 can be made to report an attacker-chosen reason — e.g. "the server is likely older than this CLI — update the server" — instead of the genuine cause. Low impact, but it is attacker-influenced text in a security diagnostic; consider printing each distinct reason at most once and preferring the most-specific refusal rather than the last.
searchedFor: read packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts refuse() and the timeout handler

samples.summary: Unauthenticated `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=…` grows an in-memory state map with a 5-minute TTL
samples.evidence: `createState` inserts into `this.states` on every CLI-mode request, before any authentication, and `cleanup()` only evicts already-expired entries — there is no size cap. `/auth/github` is covered only by the global 120 req/min throttle (app.module.ts:99), so a single IP can hold ~600 live entries and a distributed caller can grow the map without bound for 5 minutes at a time; `cleanup()` is O(n) on every insert, so the cost compounds. Pre-existing (this diff only adds the `nonce` field to the entry), and the per-entry payload is small, so I rate it a nit — but a max-size bound or an LRU would remove the vector.
searchedFor: checked auth.controller.ts for a @Throttle decorator on the `github` route (none — only callback and exchange)

verdict.reason: Verified independently: the web OAuth leg has no CSRF state binding anywhere. GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate mints a state token only under `mode === 'cli' && port` (github-auth.guard.ts:33-42); GitHubStrategy sets `opts.state` only when `__cliStateToken` is present and configures no `state: true` / no state store in super() (github.strategy.ts:43-49, 57-63), so passport-oauth2's null state store neither generates nor verifies state for browser logins. auth.controller.ts:119 gates the entire state-consumption branch on `if (stateToken)`, so a callback with only `code` falls through to createTokens + setAuthCookies + redirect (auth.controller.ts:146-150). I searched wide for a counterexample and found none: no session/CSRF middleware in main.ts:30-79, only ThrottlerGuard registered globally in app.module.ts:121-126, CliAuthStore (the repo's only state store) is called solely from the CLI branch, and the frontend's login link (packages/frontend/src/components/login-form.tsx:27) sends no state/nonce, unlike the CLI (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:40). The repository's own design doc records the gap as unfixed at docs/design/rest-api.md:384. Attack chain is complete: attacker-obtained `code` replayed via a top-level navigation in the victim's browser sets the attacker's JWT cookies (SameSite=Lax permits this, auth.controller.ts:262-268), yielding session fixation into the attacker's account. This is an auth/crypto-lane weakness (missing CSRF state binding on an authentication callback), real and blocking; being pre-existing and doc-acknowledged does not remove it.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo, and every element of the claim holds. sheets-export.ts:52 does call `formatCsv(res.data, { neutralizeFormulas: false })`, and the output is written to disk at sheets-export.ts:58. In csv.ts:74 the `neutralizeFormulas: false` branch skips `neutralizeFormula` (csv.ts:23-26) for ALL columns, not just `formula`; the only remaining transform is `NEEDS_QUOTING` (csv.ts:38), which does not match a payload such as `=cmd|'/c calc'!A0` (no comma/quote/control char), so it lands unquoted and unprefixed. The `value` column is independently attacker-settable: cells.ts:50 (`const body = formula ? { formula: value } : { value };`) and cells.ts:68-69 store an arbitrary `=`-leading string as a literal value without `--formula`. Exported rows are `{ ref, value, formula }` per the fixture at test/sheets-export.test.ts:60-61, and the test asserts only on the `formula` column, leaving `value` unconstrained. formatter.ts:61 passes `neutralizeFormulas: true` for the terminal render path, confirming the inverse risk ordering: the ephemeral path is protected, the on-disk .csv is not. The documented round-trip rationale (sheets-export.ts:46-49) justifies only keeping the `formula` column verbatim and does not cover `value`. No guard makes this unreachable, and CSV/formula injection from a co-tenant collaborator to code execution on the exporting user's machine is in the security lens's injection lane. No named refutation ground applies.

finding.summary: CSV formula neutralization is bypassable via an embedded carriage return, because `csvEscape` never quotes values containing `\r`
finding.evidence: `neutralizeFormula` (csv.ts:23) prepends `'` to a value starting with `=+-@\t\r`, but the quoting predicate at csv.ts:48 is `s.includes(',') || s.includes('"') || s.includes('\n')` — it omits `\r`. So a server-supplied value such as `ok\r=HYPERLINK("http://evil","x")` (settable by any other member of a shared workspace as a cell value, document title, or workspace name) is emitted **unquoted** with a raw CR inside the record. Spreadsheet/CSV importers that honour a bare CR as a record terminator (classic-Mac line endings; Excel and LibreOffice import paths do) split the line there, and the next record begins at column 0 with `=HYPERLINK(...)` — a formula the neutralizer never saw, because the value it inspected did not *start* with a trigger char. The new test at packages/cli/test/output.test.ts even pins the unquoted form (`expect(lines[6]).toBe("'\r=cmd")`), confirming the raw CR reaches the file. The same gap lets an attacker forge arbitrary extra rows/columns into `wafflebase sheets export out.csv` (which routes through this same `formatCsv`, packages/cli/src/commands/sheets-export.ts:46). Fix: add `\r` (and ideally `\t`) to the quoting condition so any control character forces a quoted field.

verdict.reason:
The finding's core factual claim is not present in the code. It alleges the quoting predicate is `s.includes(',') || s.includes('"') || s.includes('\n')` and omits `\r`. In fact packages/cli/src/output/csv.ts:38 defines `const NEEDS_QUOTING = /[",\n\r\t]/;` — which explicitly includes both `\r` and `\t` — and csvEscape applies it at csv.ts:75. No `includes(...)`-based predicate exists in the file; csv.ts:48 is a line inside the CsvOptions doc comment, not a quoting condition. The exact fix the finding prescribes ("add `\r` (and ideally `\t`) to the quoting condition") is already implemented, and csv.ts:28-37 is a comment documenting the identical classic-Mac-CR record-splitting rationale.

The cited test also asserts the opposite of what the finding reports: packages/cli/test/output.test.ts:148 is `expect(lines[6]).toBe('"\'\r=cmd"')` — the quoted form, not the bare `"'\r=cmd"` claimed. Additionally, output.test.ts:155-160 is a dedicated regression test ("quotes control characters so a value cannot forge a new record") feeding the reviewer's own payload shape `{ v: 'ok\r=cmd|/C calc!A0' }` and asserting it is emitted quoted at line 158.

The sheets-export variant of the claim fails too: sheets-export.ts:52 passes `neutralizeFormulas: false`, but that flag only gates the neutralizeFormula call at csv.ts:74; the NEEDS_QUOTING check at csv.ts:75 runs unconditionally outside the flag, so CR/tab are quoted on the interchange path as well. With no raw CR reaching an unquoted field on either the render path (formatter.ts:61) or the export path, the described CSV-injection / row-forgery vector does not exist.

finding.summary: The web GitHub OAuth flow still has no `state` CSRF parameter, so `/auth/github/callback` sets session cookies for whatever code is presented (login CSRF / session fixation) — the exact class this PR fixes for the CLI
finding.evidence: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` sets `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` is present (github.strategy.ts:59-62), and the `super({...})` options (github.strategy.ts:43-49) do not set `state: true`; there is no session middleware or passport state store anywhere in the backend (grep for `session(`/`state:` in main.ts/app.module.ts returns nothing). Consequently a browser (non-CLI) login sends no `state` to GitHub, and `AuthController.githubAuthCallback` reaches the web branch with `stateToken === undefined` (auth.controller.ts:119, 146-150) and unconditionally mints tokens and sets the auth cookies. Attack: the attacker starts a GitHub authorization for *their own* account, captures the resulting `code` without spending it, then makes the victim's browser issue `GET /auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>` (image/iframe/link). The backend exchanges it, sets `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` for the attacker's account in the victim's browser, and everything the victim subsequently creates or uploads lands in the attacker's workspace. `sameSite: 'lax'` (auth.controller.ts:263) does not stop a top-level GET navigation. The PR's stated thesis is login CSRF on the loopback callback; the equivalent hole on the far larger web surface is left open. Pre-existing, but it lives in the code this change edits.

verdict.reason: Verified the absence claim independently. github.strategy.ts:43-49 passes no `state`/`store` option to passport-oauth2, and authenticate() (github.strategy.ts:57-63) attaches `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` exists; that field is set exclusively in the CLI branch of GitHubAuthGuard (github-auth.guard.ts:33-42). The frontend's plain login link (login-form.tsx:27 -> GET /auth/github with no query) therefore produces an authorization request with no `state`, and no state is verified on return (passport-oauth2 uses its permissive NullStore when neither `state` nor `store` is set). In auth.controller.ts:119 the undefined `stateToken` skips the CLI path and falls through to lines 146-150, which unconditionally mint tokens and set `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh`; baseCookieOptions (auth.controller.ts:262-268) uses sameSite:'lax', which does not stop a top-level GET navigation. No compensating control exists anywhere: main.ts:30-79 registers only body-parser/cookie-parser/ValidationPipe/CORS, app.module.ts and auth.module.ts register no middleware (repo-wide grep for `configure(`/`MiddlewareConsumer` returns nothing), `express-session` is a package.json dependency (packages/backend/package.json:48) that is never imported, and there is no referer/origin/Sec-Fetch check on the callback route. The repo's own design doc (docs/design/rest-api.md:384) explicitly records this as "Open." Result: an attacker can obtain an authorization code for their own GitHub account and cause a victim's browser to load /auth/github/callback?code=..., planting the attacker's session cookies (login CSRF / session fixation) so victim-created content lands in the attacker's account. In-lane (auth/access control) and blocking.
